extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners / USPTO practitioners (training/workshop attendees)
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and examination guidance for determining whether claim limitations invoke 35 U.S.C. §112(f) (means-plus-function), construing the claim (BRI), assessing definiteness under §112(b) and written-description sufficiency under §112(a), and deciding appropriate rejections (102/103/112).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption: 'means' invokes §112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the word 'means' appears in a claim element in combination with a function, it is presumed to be a means-plus-function element to which §112(f) applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presumption that §112(f) is invoked is overcome and §112(f) will not be applied when the limitation further includes sufficient structure for performing the recited function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption: absence of 'means' ordinarily does not invoke §112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim limitation does not use 'means,' the claim limitation is presumed not to invoke §112(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption can be overcome when the limitation uses a word that is a substitute for 'means' (a generic placeholder or nonce word) that is not recognized as the name of known structure that performs the specific function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-prong MPEP 2181(I) test for invoking §112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the three-prong analysis to determine whether §112(f) applies: (A) the claim limitation uses 'means' or a substitute generic placeholder; (B) the phrase is modified by functional language (typically linked by 'for' or another linking word); and (C) the phrase is not modified by sufficient structure or material for performing the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate all three prongs. Prong B does not require the transition 'for' specifically; other linking words such as 'so that' or 'configured to' may suffice if it is clear the element is reciting a function. In some circumstances no explicit linking word is necessary if surrounding words convey the function (but those words cannot convey specific structure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify functional language (what vs. what it is)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation is functional when it recites a feature by what it does rather than by what it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional language can appear in limitations that invoke §112(f) and in limitations that do not. Limitations that do not invoke §112(f) are typically recited with some structure, material or action that defines a capability or purpose served by the recited structure, material or action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate whether words are generic placeholders or structural names
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the term used is a generic placeholder (nonce word) that conveys only function or a word that is a recognized name of structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'ink delivery means' can be interpreted as 'means for ink delivery' because 'ink delivery' conveys only function; 'keyboard means' would not be interpreted as means-plus-function because 'keyboard' has a known structural meaning. 'Keyboarding means' could be interpreted as means-plus-function with 'keyboarding' conveying pure function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) of functional language
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are given their broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification as would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If §112(f) is invoked, the BRI of the means-plus-function limitation is restricted to the corresponding structure in the supporting disclosure and its equivalents (the corresponding specification is considered part of the claim limitation). When §112(f) is not invoked and an element is recited along with a function, that element is construed as being capable of performing the function — the BRI of that element is limited by the function. Distinguish reciting a function from reciting only intended use/result: an intended use/result typically does not limit claim scope unless it imposes a structural or manipulative difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness under 35 U.S.C. §112(b): claim boundaries must be clear
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional limitations must impose clear boundaries to be definite under §112(b); claim language that merely states a result without specifying ways to achieve it is unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether one of ordinary skill in the art can determine what structure, material, or act in the claim performs the function; whether the limitation has well-defined boundaries or only expresses a problem solved or intended result; and what an anticipatory reference would need to disclose to satisfy the limitation. These considerations are illustrative, not exhaustive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corresponding-structure disclosure requirements for means-type claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When §112(f) is invoked, the specification must adequately disclose a corresponding structure, material or act that performs the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For 'means'-type claims, adequacy requires that the corresponding structure/material be: (a) disclosed so that one of ordinary skill will understand what specific structure or material the inventor identified to perform the recited function; (b) sufficient to perform the entire function recited in the claim limitation; and (c) clearly linked to the function in the written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to make a §112(b) indefiniteness rejection and record requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner determines that the boundaries of a claim are not reasonably clear, a rejection under §112(b) should be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rejection must identify the specific claim language that is indefinite and explain why that language renders the boundaries unclear. When possible, the examiner should suggest how the indefiniteness issues may be resolved to put the applicant on notice of their duty under §112(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection between indefiniteness and written-description (§112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional claim language found indefinite typically lacks an adequate written description under §112(a) because an indefinite, unbounded functional limitation may cover all ways of performing the function and indicate the inventor has not provided sufficient disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In most cases, a §112(b) rejection based on unclear functional boundaries should be accompanied by a §112(a) rejection for failure to provide a written description supporting the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-art (§102/§103) considerations for functional limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional claim language not limited to a specific structure may cover all devices/materials capable of performing the recited function, which can make §102 or §103 rejections appropriate if prior art discloses a device/material that inherently performs the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying §102/§103 rejections based on functional language, the examiner must state on the record how the functional term is being interpreted relative to the applied prior art. Consider scenarios where the prior art explicitly discloses the function, where the structure in the prior art performs the function with the same means, an equivalent means, or a different means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact-prosecution expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Under principles of compact prosecution, each claim should be examined for compliance with every statutory requirement for patentability in the initial review of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus, when a claim term/phrase renders the claim indefinite, the examiner should make a §112(b) rejection as well as any other applicable rejections (e.g., §101, §102, §103, and/or §112) in the initial action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worksheet-driven examination steps (practical checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a separate worksheet for each claim to identify functional language, apply the three-prong §112(f) test, determine BRI (depending on whether §112(f) is invoked), evaluate whether the functional language limits claim scope, assess definiteness and corresponding-structure sufficiency, and decide whether a §112(b) rejection is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific worksheet items include: (Part I) identify functional language and whether §112(f) is invoked; (Part II) state BRI if §112(f) invoked or not and identify corresponding structure if invoked; (Part III) for §112(f) limitations, answer whether specification discloses structure performing the claimed function, whether it is sufficient to perform the entire function, and whether it is clearly linked to the function; for non-§112(f) functional language, determine whether boundaries are clear to one of skill in the art; (Part IV) determine applicability of prior-art rejections and whether to issue §112(b)/§112(a) rejections and suggest how applicant could resolve unclear boundaries. The worksheet is optional but recommended for each claim.
